newsitem.title: HONG KONG: FUND VIEW - Continued high growth seen in Asia.
newsitem.headline: FUND VIEW - Continued high growth seen in Asia.

text.p: The Asian growth miracle will continue thanks to new proof of the region's productivity and efficiency, the Union Bank of Switzerland (UBS) said last week.

"Asia has had strong productivity growth and technical economic growth limits are still distant," UBS senior economist Bill Gasser, a former deputy director of research at the U.S. Federal Reserve, told reporters during a briefing on Friday.

In the latest issue of UBS International Finance, Gasser argues that a review of recent data disproves a widely cited thesis by economist Paul Krugman in 1994 that the Asian growth miracle was a myth.

Gasser and his team have reviewed data used by Krugman to argue that labour and capital inputs rather than superior productivity account for Asia's rapid growth. Krugman concluded that the region's ability to maintain past high rates of growth into the future was questionable.

"Once one accounts for the role of rapidly growing inputs in these countries, one finds little left to explain," Krugman wrote in an article in "Foreign Affairs" in December, 1994. "... future prospects for that growth are more limited than almost anyone now imagines".
Gasser said Krugman relied on studies by Alwin Young and others who compared growth in Asian countries and the rest of the world in a neo-classical economic framework.

Young's work argued that above average capital accumulation and above average labour growth largely accounted for Asia's higher growth, but that the region did not show significantly higher total factor productivity growth, or efficiency, than other countries.

"We have re-run Young's tests with more recent data and find that the high-growth Asian countries now show a significantly higher productivity growth than other countries around the world," Gasser said.
UBS said that while some Asian countries have relied more on capital accumulation than productivity to grow, all but Indonesia have enjoyed well above average productivity growth as well.
"We suspect that Young's earlier period, 1970-1985, missed some of the important recent advances in Asian technology, but data revisions may also play a role," Gasser said.
"Our results restore the 'miracle' to Asian growth, at least until better measures of capital and labour become available."
Gasser said the real "miracle" in Asia's economic expansion is the region's ability to mobilise savings, sustain strong investment and successfully adapt technology from other countries.

Cultural factors could partly explain why Asia maintains a stronger savings rate and drive towards education than other regions, but higher returns on investment in education and technology may also help to explain Asia's high growth, he said.
"If so, Asia's productivity edge may be even greater than these total factor productivity estimates suggest," Gasser said.
UBS sees a great deal of room for most Asian countries to continue turning in above average growth just by investing in available technology and further educating their people.
"We cannot guarantee that high growth will continue. But we also see no good reason in either economic theory or evidence to expect Asia to suddenly stop growing rapidly," Gasser said.
